rules.name: Small enough to grow
rules.note: live marketCap $4,798,193,125 at $76.45 (2026-09-17). Below the $5B ideal line - a genuinely small-cap regulated utility, so rate-base additions still move the needle.

rules.name: Starting yield in the usable band
rules.note: latest regular annual DPS 2.68 (FY2025, four equal 0.67 quarterlies, no specials) / price 76.45 = 3.506%. On the already-declared 2026 rate of 0.68/qtr (2.72) the forward yield is 3.56%; on ttmDividend 2.71 it is 3.54%. Comfortably inside the band and at the high end of it.

rules.name: Dividend growth above 8%/yr
rules.note: g5 = (2.68/2.16)^(1/5)-1 = 4.41%/yr. Decelerating, not steady: g10 8.37%, g5 4.41%, g3 2.62%, as the annual raise shrank from +$0.16 (2015-2022) to +$0.12, +$0.04, +$0.04. The FY2026 raise is +$0.04 again (0.67 -> 0.68, +1.5%). gMax of 11.12% is an artefact of the partial-year FY2014 base (0.84 = three post-spin-off payments) and is not usable; on the annualised 1.12 declared rate the true long-run figure is ~8.2%. Fails by a wide and widening margin.

rules.name: Payout with room left
rules.note: Regulated-utility read, as the rule allows: FY2025 FCF is -$128m (CFO $579m vs capex $707m) and FCF was negative in 8 of the 12 dividend-paying years, so dividends/FCF does not exist. Against net income: $160.7m / $264.2m = 60.8%, which is 0.8pp above the 60% ceiling - marked fail on the letter of the rule, but it is a top-of-band utility payout, not a stretched one, and it sits inside management's stated 55-65% band (0.52 in 2015 rising to 0.67 in 2024, 0.61 in 2025). The real point is that every dollar of dividend is funded externally: the equity count has gone 52.4M -> 60.2M since 2014.

rules.name: Streak long enough to prove policy
rules.note: FY2015-FY2025, each year strictly above the prior, no hold and no cut. Not window-limited: the XBRL window reaches FY2012, and FY2012-FY2013 are true zeros because ONE Gas was still an ONEOK subsidiary until the 2014-01-31 spin-off. A literal reading of the rule would say 12 (FY2014's 0.84 > FY2013's 0.00), but a first payment off a pre-spin-off zero is not an increase. priorEstimates.streak = 11 agrees with the data.

rules.name: Earnings growing at least as fast as the dividend
rules.note: FCF is negative at both 5-yr endpoints (FY2020 -$107m, FY2025 -$128m), so the CAGR is undefined and net income is used instead, as the rule allows. NI $196.4m (FY2020) -> $264.2m (FY2025) = 6.11%/yr, 1.7pp ahead of the dividend, so the payout ratio has room and has in fact fallen from 67.1% in FY2024 to 60.8% in FY2025. Caveat: part of the post-2018 earnings improvement is a lower effective tax rate (38% pre-TCJA to 14-18% now), not operating leverage.

rules.name: High return on invested capital
rules.note: FY2025 operating income $457.5m x (1-0.178) / invested capital $6.04bn = 6.23%. The series has never left 4.3%-7.1% in twelve years. This is a rate-regulated allowed return, not an excess return - by design a utility earns roughly its cost of capital, so the rule fails structurally rather than because of bad management.

rules.name: Balance sheet not competing with you
rules.note: No depreciation/amortisation tag exists anywhere in the filing extract, so EBITDA and therefore the ratio cannot be struck in any of the 14 years. Do not read the null as clean: net debt is $2.60bn against $457m of operating income, and the capital structure is roughly half debt. A gas LDC typically runs 4-5x net debt/EBITDA, i.e. this rule would very likely fail if the tag were present - flagged rather than assumed.

rules.name: Why competitors cannot take the business
rules.threshold: concrete durable mechanism, not price competition
rules.note: ONE Gas holds state-granted exclusive distribution franchises in Oklahoma, Kansas and Texas; the buried pipe network is a sunk, duplicated-at-a-loss asset and the regulator, not a rival, sets the price. No competitor can win a customer away. The mechanism is durable - but the same regulation caps the return at ~6%, which is why the moat and the low ROIC are two sides of one coin.

rules.name: Management treats the dividend as a promise
rules.threshold: no cut in FY2020/FY2021; a cut anywhere in the window fails
rules.note: FY2020 2.16 > FY2019 2.00 and FY2021 2.32 > FY2020 2.16 - the dividend was raised straight through COVID and, more tellingly, straight through Winter Storm Uri, which blew a ~$2.0bn hole in FY2021 operating cash flow. No cut, hold or special anywhere in the FY2012-FY2025 window. 2008 predates the company entirely (spun off 2014), so it is outside the window in the strongest possible sense.

analysis.verdictNote: 6 of 10 rules pass (rule 8 unassessable, excluded from the count), which maps to 'candidate' on the stated thresholds. No disqualifier applies: no cut in the window, payout 60.8% is far below 90%, and net debt/EBITDA cannot be computed so the >4x trigger cannot fire. Read as a weak candidate: both rule 3 (growth) and rule 4 (payout) fail, which is exactly what bars 'strong', and if the missing EBITDA were available rule 8 would most likely fail too, taking this to 6 of 11.
analysis.assessment: ONE Gas is a $4.8bn regulated gas LDC yielding 3.51% on the FY2025 regular dividend of $2.68 (3.56% on the already-declared 2026 rate of $2.72), with an unbroken 11-year increase streak that survived both COVID and Winter Storm Uri. The problem is the other half of the snowball: 5-yr DPS growth is 4.41% and decelerating hard to 2.62% over three years, because the last three raises were +$0.12, +$0.04 and +$0.04 - a 3.5% yield compounding at 2-4% is a bond substitute, not a compounding machine. Payout is 60.8% of net income (dividends/FCF does not exist: capex of $707m exceeded CFO of $579m in FY2025 and FCF was negative in 8 of 12 paying years), so every dividend dollar is effectively funded by the $2.60bn of net debt and by equity issuance that has grown the share count 15% since 2014. ROIC has never exceeded 7.1% and sits at 6.23%, which is the regulated allowed return - the franchise monopoly is real but the regulator caps what it earns. The thing most likely to break it is not a cut but dilution plus a rate case: if the Oklahoma/Kansas/Texas commissions grant less than the rate base needs, the equity tap funds the shortfall and per-share growth keeps grinding toward the 1.5% of this year's raise.
analysis.moat: State-granted exclusive distribution franchises over 2.2m customers in Oklahoma, Kansas and Texas: the buried pipe network cannot be economically duplicated and the regulator, not a rival, sets the price.
analysis.sectorNote: Rules 4, 7 and 8 fit a regulated utility poorly and were read accordingly. Rule 4: FCF is structurally negative because rate-base capex exceeds operating cash flow by design, so payout was assessed against net income (60.8%) and flagged as top-of-band rather than distressed. Rule 7: ROIC of 6.23% is the regulated allowed return on rate base, not evidence of a weak franchise - a utility earning 12%+ would be handing money back at its next rate case. Rule 8: no D&A tag exists in the filings, so net debt/EBITDA is null, but $2.60bn of net debt on $457m of operating income implies leverage well above the 2.5x threshold; the null is a data gap, not a clean balance sheet.
strengths: 11 consecutive increases with no hold and no cut, maintained through COVID and through Winter Storm Uri's ~$2.0bn FY2021 cash-flow shock
Yield of 3.51% (3.56% forward) at the usable end of the band, on a $4.8bn market cap that is small enough for rate-base growth to matter
Net income compounding 6.11%/yr over five years, ahead of the 4.41% dividend, so payout fell from 67.1% (FY2024) to 60.8% (FY2025)
Exclusive regulated franchises across three states - customers cannot be taken, only re-priced by regulators
Clean dividend record: no splits ever, no specials, no basis changes; filed DPS reconciles to divPaid/shares within 0.7% in all twelve paying years
risks: Dividend growth has decelerated to +$0.04/yr (+1.5% for 2026); at 3.5% yield and ~2% growth the total-return arithmetic is bond-like
FCF negative in 8 of the last 12 years - the dividend is funded by debt and equity issuance, with basic shares up 15% (52.4M to 60.2M) since 2014
Net debt/EBITDA cannot be computed (no D&A tag) but $2.60bn net debt against $457m operating income implies leverage far above the 2.5x rule
ROIC of 6.23% has never exceeded 7.1%; there is no excess return to reinvest, only allowed return
Post-2018 earnings growth is flattered by the effective tax rate falling from ~38% to 14-18%; that tailwind is spent
Regulatory risk is the single point of failure: adverse rate cases in OK/KS/TX or gas-decarbonisation policy would hit rate-base growth and the payout runway at once

analysis.assessment: NJR is a $5.4B regulated New Jersey gas LDC yielding 3.41% on the completed FY2025 dividend of $1.825 (3.59% on the current $0.48/quarter run-rate) and compounding that dividend at a metronomic 7.5%/yr over five years and 7.15% over ten - 17 straight in-window raises, none skipped in 2020 or 2021. The payout looks safe on the only basis that works here: 53.7% of FY2025 net income, with earnings up 15.5%/yr since FY2020; free cash flow is the wrong lens and in fact unavailable after FY2019, because this is a capex-heavy utility that ran negative FCF in 5 of the 11 years where it can be computed. The snowball is therefore a 3.4% yield plus ~7% growth, roughly a 10-11% total return if the rate base keeps growing and the regulator keeps allowing it - but it is a leveraged snowball: net debt/EBITDA is 4.94x, above the 4x automatic-avoid line, and net debt has tripled to $3.45B since FY2016 while ROIC sits flat at 6.7%, meaning growth is bought with debt and equity issuance rather than earned. The most likely thing to break it is a New Jersey rate case or state electrification policy that caps rate-base growth while the interest bill keeps compounding; the FY2021 payout spike to 99% of net income shows how little cushion a bad earnings year leaves. Seven of ten rules pass and nothing is broken today, but under the stated rules the >4x leverage makes this an avoid rather than the candidate the pass count alone would suggest.
analysis.moat: New Jersey Natural Gas holds a state-granted exclusive gas distribution franchise over roughly 580,000 customers with BPU-set rates on a rate base no competitor can duplicate, alongside clean-energy and storage assets.

Filed DPS never exceeds divPaid/weighted basic shares in any year (implied/filed ratio ranges 1.0010 to 1.0035, i.e. filed is always fractionally BELOW cash paid per share, the normal declared-vs-paid timing gap), so there is no year with an unexplained excess to carve out. Quarterly rate facts across 2011-2026 show four equal regular payments per year with no fifth or oversized payment. Live regularDividendIfSpecial is null and ttmDividend 2.2575 equals exactly 4 x the 0.5775 regular quarterly rate.

issues: UNITS BUG IN SOURCE TABLE: FY2010 and FY2011 report sharesBasic as 35784 and 35922 and sharesDil as 36012 and 36082, i.e. in THOUSANDS, while every other year is in whole shares. I multiplied those two years by 1000 to 35784000 and 35922000 before any per-share cross-check. Without that fix the implied DPS for 2010-2011 would come out ~1194 per share and look like a split artefact. This is the single most dangerous trap in this file.

No split occurred and none was adjusted for. splitFacts is empty, sharesBasic has no step change, and divPaid/sharesBasic matches filed DPS within 0.4% in all 17 years with share data, proving a single consistent share basis across the whole 2008-2025 window. splitAdjustments is therefore an empty array and yearsAdjusted is vacuous.

FY2008 DPS (1.19) comes from CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid, a different tag from the FY2011+ CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared series. The two tags agree exactly (1.19 vs 1.19) in both overlap years FY2011 and FY2012, so the splice is safe, but FY2008-FY2010 are cash-paid-basis not declared-basis. FY2008 also cannot be cross-checked against divPaid/shares because the table has no FY2008 row (no sharesBasic); its divPaid of 37357000 exists only in the families series.

FY2008 is present in the families series for divPaid, cfo, capex and netIncome-family tags but absent from the joined table, so fin starts at FY2009. I did not fabricate a FY2008 fin row from partial family data.

FY2009 netDebt, netDebtToEbitda and ROIC are null: debtLT is missing for that year (LongTermDebt only starts 2010-12-31; LongTermDebtNoncurrent starts 2009 but was not carried into the table). Computing them from debtCur alone would understate invested capital by roughly 430M and overstate ROIC by about 55%, so I returned null rather than a misleading number.

JUDGEMENT CALL - FY2014 and FY2015 have NO cash value at all in the table. I treated cash as 0 for netDebt and for the ROIC denominator in those two years. Justification: the filer reported cash of exactly 0 in FY2010 and FY2016 and only 2.0M in FY2013, so cash is immaterial relative to ~500-550M of debt; the effect on netDebtToEbitda is under 1%. Flagging because it is an assumption, not a filed figure.

FY2010 and FY2016 cash is a literal 0 in the source, not a missing value. I treated it as a true zero (Otter Tail did report nil cash and equivalents in those years). If it is actually a null-coerced-to-zero, netDebt for those two years is overstated by the cash balance.

JUDGEMENT CALL ON EFFECTIVE TAX - pretax is missing for FY2009 and for FY2022-FY2025 (the IncomeLossFromContinuingOperationsBeforeIncomeTaxes... family stops at 2021-12-31). I applied the specified 21% fallback for those five years. For FY2022-FY2025 I could have derived pretax as netIncome + tax (which implies roughly 20.5%, 19.1%, 17.8% and 14.4%), which would raise ROIC slightly in each of those years, but the rules specify the 21% fallback so the filed-free derivation was not used. FY2025 ROIC of 0.1084 would be about 0.1166 on a derived 14.4% rate - a 7.6% relative difference on the headline ROIC.

FY2009 effective tax cannot be computed at all: tax is NEGATIVE (-5294000, a benefit) and pretax is missing, so the 21% fallback was applied. ROIC is null for that year anyway on the missing-debt grounds above.

payoutNi is null for FY2010, FY2011 and FY2012 because NetIncomeLoss is negative (-1344000, -13243000, -5273000) - these are loss years driven by discontinued operations, not by the utility. The ratio would be negative and meaningless. Note the company held DPS flat at 1.19 straight through them rather than cutting.

FY2009 payoutNi is 1.625 (dividends 1.6x net income) and FY2013-FY2016 payoutNi sits at 0.77-0.85. These are real, not errors, but they mean net-income payout is a poor coverage signal for this name in the pre-2017 era.

payoutFcf is null in 6 of 17 years (FY2009, FY2013, FY2014, FY2015, FY2019, FY2020) because FCF = cfo - capex is NEGATIVE - capex at this regulated utility routinely exceeds operating cash flow. FY2020 is the worst at -159.6M FCF against 371.6M of capex. FY2016 payoutFcf is a valid but extreme 22.68 because FCF was only 2.127M that year. Any FCF-payout screen on OTTR needs to handle this.

fcfGrowth5 is null because the FY2020 endpoint of the 5-year FCF window is negative (-159632000); a CAGR is undefined. FCF is too cyclical here for a clean growth figure - it swings from -159.6M (2020) to +218.2M (2022) to +97.9M (2025).

gMax uses FY2008 (1.19) as the base and spans 17 years to FY2025, giving only 3.40%/yr. That understates the real dividend trajectory because the base sits inside the five-year 2009-2013 freeze. g5 (7.25%) and g3 (8.37%) are the meaningful growth rates; the dividend has visibly accelerated (FY2025 was a 12.3% raise, 1.87 to 2.10, the largest in the record).

The FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 annual DPS facts come from 10-K/A amendments rather than original 10-Ks. Values are internally consistent with the quarterly facts (4 x 0.4375 = 1.75, 4 x 0.4675 = 1.87, 4 x 0.525 = 2.10) so I used them as filed.

FY2019 has no Q1 quarterly DPS fact in dpsAllFacts (only the H1 0.70, 9M 1.05 and FY 1.40 cumulatives). Immaterial - the filed annual figure of 1.40 was used and is confirmed by the 1.05 nine-month cumulative implying a 0.35 quarterly rate.

FY2026 data exists (Q1 and Q2 at 0.5775/qtr) but FY2026 is incomplete and is excluded from both dps and fin. No 4x-the-latest-rate extrapolation was performed for any year since every year in the series has a filed annual figure.

Revenue uses the Revenues tag for all 18 years for consistency; RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax (2019+) and ...IncludingAssessedTax (2020-2023) exist as alternates and may differ slightly for the overlap years.

cfo uses NetCashProvidedByUsedInOperatingActivities throughout. The continuing-operations variant differs materially in several years (FY2012: 155.0M vs 233.5M total; FY2011: 93.7M vs 104.4M) so FCF and payoutFcf for FY2009-FY2017 would change substantially on a continuing-ops basis. Total-company basis was used because it is the only series covering all 18 years.

debtCur uses LongTermDebtCurrent. ShortTermBorrowings is a separate 15-point series that was NOT added into net debt, so net debt may be understated in years with revolver draws. FY2022, FY2023 and FY2024 show debtCur of exactly 0, which is plausible for this filer but sits alongside a populated ShortTermBorrowings tag.
priorEstimates were materially wrong on all three numbers (growth5y 9 vs actual 7.25; streak 14 vs actual 12; payoutPctFcf 30 vs actual 90 in FY2025) and have been fully replaced.

issues.detail: Cash is entirely ABSENT from the raw table for 2014-12-31 and 2015-12-31 (unlike 2010 and 2016, where cash is a literal 0). The record substituted cash = 0 to compute netDebt (498,892,000 and 550,911,000), netDebtToEbitda (3.165458, 3.248737) and the ROIC denominators. That is an assumed input, not a filed figure, and the derivation rules say to return null when a component is not derivable. The record discloses it as a judgement call, so it is transparent, but the two netDebt figures are not fully filed-derived.
issues.suggested: Either set fin[2014].netDebt, netDebtToEbitda and fin[2015].netDebt, netDebtToEbitda to null with the reason 'cash missing from source', or keep the current values but label basis as assumed-zero-cash. ROIC for 2014 (0.071937) and 2015 (0.068995) is an upper bound; any positive cash balance lowers the denominator and RAISES ROIC slightly.

issues.detail: Net debt uses debtCur = LongTermDebtCurrent only. The source carries a separate 15-point ShortTermBorrowings series spanning 2009-2025 that was not added. This matters most in FY2022, FY2023 and FY2024, where LongTermDebtCurrent is exactly 0 while a ShortTermBorrowings tag is populated, so net debt (and netDebtToEbitda 1.465738 / 1.247572 / 1.331805) may be understated and ROIC correspondingly overstated in those years. The record flags this in dataQuality but still publishes the unadjusted figures as if complete.
issues.suggested: Not recomputable from this file (the debtCur family has no series block, only candidate metadata), so I cannot quantify it. Recommend pulling the ShortTermBorrowings series and re-deriving netDebt = LongTermDebt + LongTermDebtCurrent + ShortTermBorrowings - cash for FY2022-FY2024 before relying on the 1.25-1.42x leverage figures.

A continuing-operations variant exists for 2009-2017 and differs materially (FY2012: 155.0M vs the 233.5M used; FY2011: 93.7M vs 104.4M), so FCF and payoutFcf across that stretch are on a total-company basis that includes discontinued operations. The choice is reasonable (it is the only 18-year series) and disclosed, but the pre-2018 payoutFcf figures are not comparable to a continuing-ops view.

For Otter Tail - a regulated electric utility plus a manufacturing/plastics segment (live.sector Industrials, ~3.7B cap) that earned outsized plastics profits in 2021-2022 - mid-to-high single digit dividend growth accelerating into a 12.3% FY2025 raise is squarely plausible. No red flag.

Divergence vs priorEstimates (g5 9 -> 7.25; streak 14 -> 12; payoutPctFcf 30 -> 90) - each is explicitly addressed in notes/dataQuality with a derivation (5-yr CAGR arithmetic, the 2009-2013 flat-at-1.19 stretch that caps the in-data streak at 12, and capex >= CFO at the regulated utility driving FCF payout to 0.90 in FY2025 and negative FCF in 6 of 17 years). issues.detail: Arithmetic error in the stated justification for 'no specials': both the notes and specials.note assert 'live ttmDividend 2.2575 = 4 x the 0.5775 Q1/Q2-2026 declared rate'. 4 x 0.5775 = 2.31, not 2.2575. The true decomposition is one 0.525 (Q4-2025 payment) plus three 0.5775 payments = 2.2575, i.e. the TTM straddles the raise. The conclusion (no special dividend) still holds - in fact the correct decomposition is stronger evidence, since it matches a mid-window raise exactly - but the stated evidence as written is wrong and would fail any downstream re-verification.
issues.suggested: Replace with: 'live ttmDividend 2.2575 = 0.525 (one pre-raise quarter) + 3 x 0.5775 (post-raise quarters), exactly the regular run-rate across the Q1-2026 raise; the forward annualised rate is 4 x 0.5775 = 2.31.'

issues.detail: The record characterises OTTR flatly as 'the regulated utility' when explaining capex >= CFO and thin FCF. Live data classifies it Industrials and priorEstimates flags 'plastics-cycle'. Otter Tail is a hybrid: a regulated electric utility plus Manufacturing and Plastics segments, and the 2021-2022 earnings/FCF surge (netIncome 95.9M -> 176.8M -> 284.2M, ebitda 229.9M -> 483.0M) is plastics-driven, not rate-base driven. The capex explanation for negative FCF is still correct, but the one-sided framing understates the cyclicality behind the post-2021 payout ratios (payoutNi falling 0.63 -> 0.24) and behind the fcfGrowth5 null.
issues.suggested: Amend the note to: 'Otter Tail is a hybrid - regulated electric utility (rate-base capex regularly at or above CFO) plus Manufacturing and Plastics segments; the FY2021-FY2022 step-up in netIncome/EBITDA and the drop in payoutNi to ~0.24 is plastics-cycle driven and should not be read as a durable payout floor.'

rules.name: Small enough to grow
rules.note: Live marketCap 3,737,844,423 at $89.03 (2026-09-17). Comfortably in the ideal band; implied shares 41.98M match coverSharesOutstanding 41,985,580, so the cap is clean.

rules.name: Starting yield in the usable band
rules.note: Latest regular annual DPS on the current basis = 4 x $0.5775 (Q1/Q2-2026 declared rate) = $2.31; 2.31/89.03 = 2.59%. On the completed FY2025 DPS of $2.10 the yield is 2.36%, and on live TTM $2.2575 it is 2.54%. No specials to strip - regularDividendIfSpecial is null and TTM = 0.525 + 3 x 0.5775, exactly a mid-window raise.

rules.name: Dividend growth above 8%/yr
rules.note: FAIL, but narrowly and improving. (2.10/1.48)^(1/5)-1 = 7.249%. The 3-yr CAGR is 8.37% and the FY2025 raise was 12.3% (1.87 -> 2.10), the largest in the 18-year record; the next declared step (0.525 -> 0.5775) is another 10.0%. No split adjustment applies (splitFacts empty, share count smooth 35.5M -> 41.9M).

rules.name: Payout with room left
rules.note: FAIL on the primary test: FY2025 dividends 88.064M vs FCF 97.917M = 89.9%, and the 3-yr average (239.4M / 309.4M) is still 77.4%. The utility carve-out does not fully apply because FY2025 FCF is positive (+97.9M), but the spirit of it does: capex has run at or above CFO in 7 of the last 17 years (FY2020 FCF -159.6M on 371.6M capex), so FCF payout is structurally noisy here. On net income the payout is a comfortable 31.9% (88.064M / 275.893M), and on CFO it is 22.8%. Read honestly: the dividend is covered by earnings and operating cash, not by free cash flow after rate-base capex.

rules.name: Streak long enough to prove policy
rules.note: Twelve consecutive increases, FY2014 (1.19 -> 1.21) through FY2025 (2.10). NOT window-limited: the data starts at FY2008 and the streak-breaking events are visible in-window - DPS was held flat at exactly 1.19 for five straight years, FY2009-FY2013. The prior research estimate of 14 is therefore wrong, not merely longer, and 12 is used.

rules.name: Earnings growing at least as fast as the dividend
rules.note: FCF basis is unusable: the FY2020 endpoint is negative (-159.6M), so fcfGrowth5 is null by construction. On net income, 95.851M (FY2020) -> 275.893M (FY2025) = 23.5%/yr, far above the 7.25% dividend CAGR. Caveat: the FY2020 base is pre-plastics-boom and FY2022 was the cycle peak (NI 284.2M, EBITDA 483.0M); FY2023-FY2025 NI is roughly flat at 294/302/276M, so the true underlying rate is much lower than 23.5%.

rules.name: High return on invested capital
rules.note: FY2025 ROIC 10.84% on the specified 21% tax fallback (pretax is absent from the source for FY2022-FY2025). Deriving the effective rate as tax/(NI+tax) gives ~14.4% for FY2025 and lifts ROIC only to ~11.7% - still short of 12%. The trend is downward off the plastics peak: 16.0% (2022), 14.7% (2023), 13.0% (2024), 10.8% (2025). Net debt excludes a populated ShortTermBorrowings series, so invested capital is if anything understated and true ROIC slightly lower.

rules.name: Balance sheet not competing with you
rules.note: FY2025 net debt 657.3M (LT debt 963.6M + current 80.0M - cash 386.2M) over EBITDA 463.8M = 1.42x, and it has sat between 1.25x and 1.47x for four years - a genuinely conservative sheet for a rate-base utility. Caveat: ShortTermBorrowings was not added in, so this is a lower bound; even a material revolver draw would leave it well under 2.5x.

rules.name: Why competitors cannot take the business
rules.threshold: concrete durable mechanism, not price competition
rules.note: True for roughly half the company. Otter Tail Power is a state-franchised regulated electric monopoly across Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota - nobody can build a parallel grid and the commissions set an allowed return on the rate base, which is why capex of 288-372M/yr is a growth engine rather than a leak. The Manufacturing and Plastics segments have no such protection: PVC pipe is a commodity whose 2021-2022 super-margins were a cycle, not a moat.

rules.name: Management treats the dividend as a promise
rules.threshold: no cut in FY2020/FY2021; any cut/suspension in window fails
rules.note: FY2020 and FY2021 were both increases (+5.7%, +5.4%). There is no cut or suspension anywhere in the 2008-2025 window. Stronger evidence than that: the board held the dividend at 1.19 straight through FY2010-FY2012 when reported net income was NEGATIVE on discontinued-operations losses, paying out 1.6x earnings in FY2009 rather than cutting. FY2008 itself is inside this dataset (1.19), so the pre-crisis record is not a blind spot here, though pre-2008 history is.

analysis.assessment: Otter Tail is a $3.7B hybrid - a franchised electric monopoly in MN/ND/SD bolted to a commodity PVC pipe maker - offering a 2.6% starting yield on the current $2.31 annualised rate, growing dividends at 7.25% over five years and accelerating (12.3% in FY2025, another 10.0% declared for 2026). The snowball is therefore mid-single-digit yield-plus-growth of roughly 10%, funded by a dividend that takes only 31.9% of net income and 22.8% of operating cash flow but a full 89.9% of free cash flow, because rate-base capex of $288M swallows three quarters of the $386M of CFO. Leverage is genuinely low at 1.42x net debt/EBITDA after four years of plastics windfall paid down the sheet, and the 12-year increase streak is real and in-data, broken only by the honest five-year freeze at $1.19 through 2009-2013 - a period in which management held rather than cut through three loss years. What most likely breaks it is the plastics cycle normalising: ROIC has already slid from 16.0% in FY2022 to 10.84% in FY2025 and net income from $302M to $276M, and if PVC margins revert toward pre-2021 levels the $88M dividend is being paid out of a utility that does not by itself generate free cash. It fails rules 3, 4 and 7 - growth just under 8%, FCF payout near 90%, ROIC just under 12% - so it is a solid candidate, not a strong one.
analysis.sectorNote: Rules 4, 6 and 7 fit this business model badly. As a regulated utility, Otter Tail deliberately spends its operating cash on rate base (capex >= CFO in 7 of the last 17 years; FCF negative in 6), so dividends/FCF is a poor coverage measure - I report 89.9% as the rule requires but read coverage off net income (31.9%) and CFO (22.8%), which is how a utility should be judged. Rule 6 likewise falls back to net income because the FY2020 FCF endpoint is negative and a CAGR is undefined. Conversely, the Manufacturing/Plastics half is NOT a utility, and its 2021-2022 cycle peak is what flatters the rule-6 net income CAGR and inflated the FY2022 ROIC of 16.0%; neither should be extrapolated.
analysis.moat: A state-franchised regulated electric monopoly across Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota - a grid no competitor can duplicate and a commission-set return on a growing rate base - which funds and cushions a higher-margin but genuinely competitive PVC pipe manufacturer.
strengths: Market cap $3.74B sits in the ideal < $5B band with room to compound
12 consecutive increases proven in-data (not window-limited), with the dividend held rather than cut through the FY2010-FY2012 loss years
Net debt/EBITDA 1.42x, below 2.5x for four straight years - the balance sheet is not competing for the dividend
Dividend takes only 31.9% of net income and 22.8% of CFO, leaving real room on the measures that fit a utility
Dividend growth is accelerating, not fading: 5-yr 7.25%, 3-yr 8.37%, FY2025 +12.3%, 2026 rate +10.0%
Regulated utility half is a franchise monopoly whose capex is a return-earning rate base rather than a cash leak
risks: Plastics cycle reversion: ROIC 16.0% (FY2022) -> 10.84% (FY2025) and revenue down three years running from $1.47B to $1.30B
Dividends absorb 89.9% of FY2025 free cash flow; FCF has been negative in 6 of the last 17 years and any capex step-up puts the raise on the balance sheet
ROIC 10.84% is below the 12% bar even on a favourable derived tax rate (~11.7%)
5-yr DPS CAGR 7.25% is below the 8% bar; only the 3-yr and current rate clear it
Reported net debt excludes a populated ShortTermBorrowings series and FY2014/FY2015 assume zero cash, so leverage is a lower bound
Earnings quality: the rule-6 pass rests on a FY2020 net income base that predates the plastics windfall; FY2023-FY2025 net income is flat to down

Kept in substance, refined for accuracy. Prior sentence: 'Regulated electric utility funding a high-margin PVC pipe manufacturer.' normalised.dpsMethod: Filed annual DPS tag used directly (rule a): CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid with ~364-365 day durations, FY2009-FY2025, 17 continuous points, all from 10-K/10-K/A. No split adjustment applied to any year (see splitAdjustments: empty). Cross-checked every year against divPaid / weighted-average basic shares: all 17 years agree within 0.8% (max deviation FY2010 -0.80%, FY2019 -0.74%), confirming a single consistent share basis across the whole window and no special dividends. The alternative tag CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared (FY2021-FY2024) agrees exactly for FY2022-FY2024 and differs only trivially for FY2021 (1.1075 declared vs 1.1080 cash paid); cash-paid was kept as primary for series continuity. Quarterly rate facts in dpsAllFacts independently confirm the annual totals (e.g. FY2022 = 0.29+0.29+0.29+0.3125 = 1.1825; FY2025 = 0.34 x 4 = 1.36 vs 1.38 filed, the difference being the Q4-2024 0.34 / Q4-2025 0.36 rate-change timing on a cash-paid basis).

specials.note: No special dividends found. The filed DPS never exceeds divPaid/sharesBasic by more than 0.8% in any of the 17 years, and every quarterly fact in dpsAllFacts is an ordinary quarterly rate on a smooth step-up path (0.1800 -> 0.3600 per quarter over 2010-2026). PaymentsOfDividends (FY2009-FY2012, ~$206-208k) and PaymentsOfDividendsPreferredStockAndPreferenceStock / DividendsPreferredStockCash ($76k in FY2025) are PREFERRED dividends, not common specials; they were excluded from divPaid, which uses PaymentsOfDividendsCommonStock throughout.

FY2024 and FY2025 have no D&A value in the table (the DepreciationDepletionAndAmortization series ends FY2023; Depreciation and DepreciationAndAmortization candidate tags exist through FY2025 but no series was supplied), so EBITDA and netDebt/EBITDA are null for both years, including the latest year.

normalised.notes: Middlesex Water (CIK 0000066004), calendar fiscal year ending 12-31, 17 years of continuous filed data FY2009-FY2025. This is a clean, unambiguous dividend record: filed annual DPS exists for every year, no splits occurred in the window, no special dividends were paid, and the divPaid/shares cross-check agrees with the filed DPS to within 0.8% in all 17 years. Regular DPS compounded from $0.713 (FY2009) to $1.380 (FY2025), a 4.21%/yr 16-year CAGR that has ACCELERATED over time: 5.93% over 10 years, 5.80% over 5 years, 5.28% over 3 years. The pace of increases stepped up sharply around FY2016 - annual raises were a flat ~$0.01/yr from FY2009 to FY2015 (roughly 1.3%/yr) and have run 4-7%/yr since. The prior 6% five-year growth estimate is close (actual 5.80%); the prior 53-year streak is consistent with but unverifiable from this window, which shows 16 consecutive increases with no cut or hold and no 2020 cut. The prior 60% payout-of-FCF estimate is wrong in kind, not just degree: FCF is negative in every year it can be computed (FY2020-FY2024), because capex ran 1.3-2.0x operating cash flow while the company built out rate base; the dividend is funded from a mix of operating cash, debt and DRIP/equity issuance, and shares outstanding have risen ~35% since FY2009. Payout on net income, the usable coverage metric, sits at 58.2% in FY2025 and has averaged ~53% over the last five years. Live FMP TTM dividend of $1.44 is consistent with the Q1/Q2-2026 rate of $0.36 already visible in the 10-Q facts, implying FY2026 DPS of about $1.44-1.46 and a ~4.3% forward raise. Leverage has roughly doubled over the window (netDebt/EBITDA 2.5x in FY2016 to 5.2x in FY2021, 4.1x in FY2022) alongside the capex program; FY2024-FY2025 leverage cannot be computed for lack of a D&A fact, and FY2023's 10.5x is an artifact of a mis-tagged current-maturity figure, not a real balance-sheet event. Confidence is medium overall: the dividend series itself is high confidence, but capex, D&A, FY2025 revenue and the FY2023 debt split are materially incomplete or defective.

issues.detail: The record itself concludes FY2023 debtCur = 364,736,000 is 'almost certainly a mis-tagged fact' (21x FY2022's 17,462k, 47x FY2024's 7,711k, and roughly equal to that year's debtLT of 358,153k — i.e. the filer appears to have double-tagged the whole long-term balance as current), yet still publishes netDebt 720,499,000 and netDebtToEbitda 10.493 as ordinary values in the fin array. Anything consuming fin without reading dataQuality will read a leverage spike from 4.06x to 10.49x and back to ~4x as a real balance-sheet event. The same inflated denominator (1,143,490k invested capital) also depresses FY2023 ROIC to 0.0332. I verified the arithmetic is faithful to the prescribed formula, so this is a disclosure/propagation concern, not a computation error. Note also that the debtCur candidates ShortTermBorrowings (14 pts, through FY2023) and LongTermDebtAndCapitalLeaseObligationsCurrent (6 pts, FY2019-FY2024) both cover FY2023 but have no supplied series, so no corrected figure is derivable from this file.
issues.suggested: Keep netDebt 720,499,000 (formula applied verbatim) but null netDebtToEbitda for FY2023 with the reason recorded, or add an explicit per-row flag such as suspect:true, rather than leaving 10.493 to be read as a real reading. Do NOT substitute an invented current-maturity figure — none is derivable here.

issues.detail: The FY2025 reconciliation is stated incorrectly even though the conclusion is right. The text says 'FY2025 = 0.34 x 4 = 1.36 vs 1.38 filed, the difference being the Q4-2024 0.34 / Q4-2025 0.36 rate-change timing'. Only three FY2025 quarterly cash-paid facts exist (Q1/Q2/Q3 at 0.34); there is no fourth 0.34 fact, so the 4x extrapolation is the record's own assumption, not filed data. The filed annual 1.38 minus 3 x 0.34 implies a Q4-2025 cash-paid rate of exactly 0.36 — which is independently confirmed by the 2026-Q1 and 2026-Q2 facts at 0.36 and by the identical Q4 step in FY2024 (0.325 x 3 + 0.34 = 1.315) and FY2023 declared (0.3125 x 3 + 0.325 = 1.2625). Stated as a residual, the quarterlies reconcile to 1.38 with zero gap.
issues.suggested: Replace with: 'FY2025 quarterly cash-paid facts are Q1-Q3 = 0.34 each; filed annual 1.38 implies Q4 = 0.36, matching the 2026-Q1/Q2 rate facts and the same Q4 rate-step pattern seen in FY2023 and FY2024. Quarterlies reconcile exactly, confirming the annual figure is wholly regular.'

issues.detail: yearsCovered = 17 counts data points, while gMax is computed over 16 fiscal-year intervals (FY2009 -> FY2025) — the record's own notes say '4.21%/yr 16-year CAGR' and 'gMax spans 16 fiscal years'. Both are defensible readings of the label, but the field and the CAGR it sits beside use different conventions, which invites an off-by-one when a consumer reconstructs the exponent.
issues.suggested: Either set yearsCovered = 16 to match the gMax exponent, or leave 17 and state in the field's documentation that it is a point count, not a span. My recomputation confirms gMax 4.2136% uses N=16, which is correct per the CAGR rule.

issues.detail: FY2023 netDebt $720,499,000 and netDebt/EBITDA 10.493x are carried in the record as computed values even though the record itself identifies the input (debtCur $364,736,000) as almost certainly mis-tagged - 21x FY2022 and 47x FY2024. This is disclosed in dataQuality, so it is not an unexplained divergence, but externally it is incoherent: a ~$1bn-cap water utility did not carry 10.5x leverage in FY2023 and then return to ~4x in FY2024 with no equity raise, dividend action or credit event. Any downstream consumer that reads fin[] without reading the issues array will show a false leverage spike and a depressed FY2023 ROIC (3.32%).

A FY2022/FY2024-consistent current maturity of roughly $10-18m implies netDebt near $366-374m and netDebt/EBITDA near 5.3-5.5x on the FY2023 EBITDA of $68,665,000; FY2023 ROIC on that basis would be meaningfully above the stated 3.32%.

rules.name: Small enough to grow
rules.note: Live marketCap $1,061,100,009 at $56.31 (asOf 2026-09-17). Comfortably in the ideal band - a ~$1bn regulated water utility is small enough that incremental rate base moves the needle.

rules.name: Starting yield in the usable band
rules.note: Latest regular annual DPS $1.38 (FY2025, filed) / $56.31 = 2.451%. On the live forward rate (TTM $1.44, quarterly already stepped to $0.36) the yield is 2.56%. No specials in the series, so no adjustment needed.

rules.name: Dividend growth above 8%/yr
rules.note: FY2020 $1.041 -> FY2025 $1.380 = 5.80%/yr. 3-yr 5.28%, 10-yr 5.93%, 16-yr 4.21%. Growth is steady and has accelerated from ~1.3%/yr pre-FY2016, but mid-single digits is structurally what a regulated rate-base compounder delivers. Fails by 2.2pp.

rules.name: Payout with room left
rules.note: SECTOR ADJUSTMENT: FCF is negative in all five years it can be computed (FY2020 -$52.3m to FY2024 -$15.9m) because capex ran 1.3-2.0x CFO on rate-base build, so payout-of-FCF is meaningless here and is assessed on net income per the rule. $24.9m dividends / $42.8m FY2025 net income = 58.2%, inside the 20-60% band; five-year average ~53%. Coverage is real but the headroom is thin at the top of the band.

rules.name: Streak long enough to prove policy, short enough to still be fast
rules.note: Filed data shows 16 consecutive increases FY2010-FY2025 with no hold or cut, but the streak runs to the first year of the XBRL window (FY2009) so it is window-limited. Prior research streak of 53 years is plausible and not contradicted - Middlesex has raised since the early 1970s. Using 53 the rule FAILS on the upper bound: this is a mature, fully-policied payer, not a fast young grower. On the 16-year data streak alone it would pass; I used the research figure because it is the true policy history.

rules.name: Earnings growing at least as fast as the dividend
rules.note: FCF endpoints are negative (FY2020 -$52.3m) and FY2025 FCF is not derivable, so net income is used and said so: $38.4m (FY2020) -> $42.8m (FY2025) = 2.19%/yr, less than half the dividend's 5.80%. Earnings are being lapped by the dividend; the payout ratio has therefore drifted from 47.3% to 58.2% over the same five years.

rules.name: High return on invested capital
rules.note: FY2025 ROIC = operating income $54.4m x (1 - 4,821/47,643) / invested capital $878.0m = 5.57%. The series sits 3.3-6.7% across every computable year. This is the allowed regulated return on a rate base, not an economic moat return - the business earns roughly its cost of capital by design.

rules.name: Balance sheet not competing with you
rules.note: FY2024/FY2025 EBITDA is not computable (no D&A fact) and FY2023's 10.49x is an artifact of a mis-tagged $364.7m current maturity. The last clean reading is FY2022 4.06x, and the trend is one way: 2.54x (FY2016) -> 4.47x (FY2019) -> 5.16x (FY2021) -> 4.06x (FY2022). FY2025 net debt is $383.9m; against FY2023 EBITDA of $68.7m or a generous $80m that is 4.8-5.6x. Above 4x on every reasonable reading - this triggers the avoid override.

rules.name: Why competitors cannot take the business
rules.value: State-granted exclusive franchise over buried network
rules.note: A second water utility cannot lay a duplicate distribution network into Middlesex's New Jersey and Delaware territories; service areas are exclusive franchises granted by the NJ BPU and Delaware PSC, and the ~$1.5bn of pipe already in the ground is the barrier. Nobody competes on price for tap water.

rules.name: Management treats the dividend as a promise
rules.threshold: no cut in FY2020/FY2021; cut anywhere in window fails
rules.note: FY2020 DPS $1.041 > FY2019 $0.976 and FY2021 $1.108 > FY2020 - raised straight through COVID. No cut, hold or suspension anywhere in the FY2009-FY2025 window. 2008 is outside the XBRL window and cannot be checked from this data.

analysis.sectorNote: Regulated water utility. Rule 4 cannot be read on FCF: capex ran 1.3-2.0x operating cash flow every computable year (FY2020-FY2024) to fund rate-base growth, so FCF was negative in all of them and payout-of-FCF is null for the entire 17-year record. Payout is therefore assessed against net income (58.2% FY2025, ~53% five-year average), which is the meaningful coverage measure for a business that funds plant with debt and DRIP equity by regulatory design. Rule 7 is likewise structurally unwinnable: a regulated utility earns an authorised return on rate base (~5-7% ROIC here), so the low figure is a feature of the model, not evidence of a bad operator - but it is still a real constraint on the compounding rate an owner receives. Rule 8's 2.5x threshold is tight for a utility, where 4-5x is industry-normal; I have still marked it fail and let it trigger the avoid override, because the screen's own override language is unconditional and MSEX's leverage has genuinely doubled over the window.
analysis.moat: Regulated water and wastewater franchises in New Jersey and Delaware: the distribution network is already buried, service territories are exclusive grants from the NJ BPU and Delaware PSC, and no rival can lay a second set of pipes to compete for the same tap.
strengths: Flawless dividend record: 16 consecutive filed increases FY2010-FY2025, raised through COVID, no cut or hold anywhere in the window, and a research streak of ~53 years behind it.
Growth has accelerated, not decayed: raises ran a flat ~$0.01/yr (1.3%/yr) through FY2015 and 4-7%/yr since, giving 5.80% over five years and 5.93% over ten.
$1.06bn market cap in the ideal small-cap band, with a genuine state-granted franchise moat and a 2.45% starting yield inside the usable band.
Dividend series is high-confidence: filed annual DPS every year, no splits, no specials, and divPaid/shares reconciles to the filed figure within 0.8% in all 17 years.
risks: Leverage: net debt $383.9m at FY2025 against ~$69-80m of EBITDA is roughly 4.8-5.6x, versus 2.54x in FY2016. FY2024/FY2025 cannot be computed exactly for want of a D&A fact, but every readable year since FY2019 is above 4x.

Dividend is outgrowing earnings: net income CAGR 2.19% over five years against DPS 5.80%, pushing payout from 47.3% (FY2020) to 58.2% (FY2025). Another five years of that arithmetic puts payout near 70%.

The dividend is not funded from free cash flow in any computable year - FCF was -$52.3m to -$15.9m FY2020-FY2024 - so it depends on continued access to debt and DRIP/ATM equity. Shares outstanding are up ~35% since FY2009, diluting per-share growth.

Single-jurisdiction regulatory risk: essentially all earnings depend on NJ BPU and Delaware PSC rate cases. An adverse or delayed rate order with capex already sunk is the direct mechanism by which the raise slows.

Data gaps in the latest year: FY2025 capex, revenue and D&A are all absent, so FCF, FCF margin and leverage cannot be computed for the current year. Confidence on everything except the dividend series is medium.
analysis.assessment: Middlesex Water is an impeccable payer attached to a balance sheet that is quietly competing with the shareholder. The snowball on offer is a 2.45% starting yield ($1.38 FY2025 DPS on a $56.31 price, 2.56% on the $1.44 live forward rate) growing 5.80%/yr, which is an ~8.3% total-return arithmetic before multiple change - respectable, but a full 2.2pp of dividend growth short of the screen's bar and nowhere near a fast compounder. The payout runway looks adequate at 58.2% of net income, but that is the wrong-looking number twice over: it is measured on earnings because free cash flow was negative every single computable year (-$52.3m in FY2020 through -$15.9m in FY2024, capex at 1.3-2.0x CFO), and it has drifted up from 47.3% in FY2020 because net income grew 2.19%/yr while the dividend grew 5.80%/yr. Return on invested capital of 5.57% confirms this is a regulated annuity earning its authorised return, not a business creating surplus value, and net debt of $383.9m against $69-80m of EBITDA (4.8-5.6x, versus 2.54x in FY2016 and 4.06x at the last clean FY2022 reading) is the thing most likely to break it - a rate case that comes in short or a credit-driven pause on the capex-funded dividend would end a 53-year streak that the company has otherwise defended without a single flinch, including straight through 2020.

screenFields.payoutBasis: net income (FY2025 $24.9m dividends / $42.8m NI) - payout-of-FCF is not computable in any year because FCF is negative throughout the rate-base build

estimateCorrections.why: Wrong in kind, not just degree. The prior 60% was a payout-of-free-cash-flow figure; MSEX has negative FCF in every year it can be computed (FY2020 -$52.3m, FY2021 -$46.4m, FY2022 -$30.0m, FY2023 -$37.4m, FY2024 -$15.9m), so a payout-of-FCF percentage does not exist for this company. The replacement 58.2% is payout of net income for FY2025, which is the correct coverage measure for a regulated utility funding rate base with debt and DRIP equity. The basis change matters more than the 1.8pp move.

Refinement only, 0.2pp - below the 3pp materiality bar but worth carrying because it is now a filed-data figure rather than an estimate: FY2020 $1.041 -> FY2025 $1.380 = 5.80%/yr, verified against 17 continuous 10-K DPS facts with no splits and no specials.

Not previously carried. Leverage is the binding constraint on this holding and the screen was blind to it: 2.54x (FY2016) -> 4.47x (FY2019) -> 5.16x (FY2021) -> 4.06x (FY2022, last clean reading). FY2023's 10.49x is a mis-tagged current-maturity artifact and FY2024/FY2025 are not computable for want of a D&A fact, so 4.06x is the most recent defensible figure; FY2025 net debt of $383.9m implies something closer to 4.8-5.6x.

Not previously carried. FY2025 ROIC of 5.57% (and 3.3-6.7% across the whole computable series) puts MSEX far below the screen's 12% bar and makes clear the return here is an authorised regulated return, not an economic-moat return.

No change, but the provenance is now explicit: filed data confirms only 16 consecutive increases (FY2010-FY2025), and that streak reaches the first year of the XBRL window, so it is window-limited rather than contradicting the 53-year research figure. The research figure is retained for the screen, and it is what causes rule 5 to fail on its upper bound.

stocks.m: Stepan's scale and plant network in surfactants plus formulations qualified into customers' consumer-product recipes create switching friction, but the product still clears on price against commodity feedstock costs - which is why ROIC fell from ~15% to ~3%.

normalised.dpsMethod: Filed annual DPS tag with ~1-year duration (rule a): CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid, FY duration 364-365 days, form 10-K, used verbatim for FY2010-FY2025 (already on today's post-split basis in every filing that reports it). FY2009 has no CashPaid fact, so it comes from the only other annual tag, CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared FY2009 = 0.90, divided by 2 for the 2013 2-for-1 split -> 0.45. The two tags are identical in every overlapping year (FY2010: declared 0.98 = 2 x cash-paid 0.49; FY2011: declared 1.06 = 2 x 0.53), so the declared series is a safe source for FY2009 once rebased. Quarterly facts were used only as a check: FY2025 = 0.385 x 3 (Q1-Q3, 9M = 1.155) + 0.395 in Q4 = 1.55, matching the filed annual; the Q1/Q2 2026 rate of 0.395 x 4 = 1.58 equals live ttmDividend.

splitAdjustments.note: 2-for-1 split. splitFacts carry ratio 2 at 2012-12-31 (10-K), 2013-03-31 (10-Q) and 2013-12-31 (10-K); the exact effective date is not in the data, but the ratio first appears on the FY2012 10-K, so the split was declared/effected around early 2013 and that 10-K restated FY2012, FY2011 and FY2010. Evidence for adjusting FY2009 ONLY: (i) sharesBasic steps from 9,870,000 in FY2009 to 20,326,000 in FY2010 - a clean ~2x break exactly at the edge of the three-year restatement window; (ii) FY2009 common cash dividends 8,802,000 / 9,870,000 shares = 0.8918, self-consistent with the filed FY2009 declared DPS of 0.90, i.e. old basis; (iii) FY2010 common cash dividends 9,823,000 / 20,326,000 = 0.4833, self-consistent with the filed cash-paid DPS of 0.49, i.e. already new basis; (iv) 0.90 is ~2x its neighbours on an otherwise smooth 0.45 -> 0.49 -> 0.53 trend. Adjustments applied: FY2009 DPS 0.90 / 2 = 0.45 and FY2009 sharesBasic 9,870,000 x 2 = 19,740,000. No other year touched. Note the FY2010 and FY2011 CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared facts (0.98, 1.06) ARE old-basis leftovers from pre-split filings, but they are not used - the post-split CashPaid facts (0.49, 0.53) are.

specials.note: No special dividends found. Every year's filed DPS sits slightly BELOW divPaid/sharesBasic (never above), which is the opposite of the special-dividend signature. dpsAllFacts contains no off-cycle or oversized per-share fact; the quarterly cash-paid rates step smoothly (0.275 -> 0.305 -> 0.335 -> 0.365 -> 0.375 -> 0.385 -> 0.395). live.regularDividendIfSpecial is null and live.ttmDividend 1.58 = 4 x the current 0.395 regular quarterly rate. PreferredStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid 1.375 exists through 2013 but is a preferred-share dividend, not a common special.

issues: SPLIT JUDGEMENT: only FY2009 was rebased for the 2013 2-for-1 split (DPS 0.90 -> 0.45; sharesBasic 9,870,000 -> 19,740,000). FY2010-FY2012 were NOT divided, because the FY2012 10-K that first carries the split ratio restated those three years - confirmed by sharesBasic jumping 9.87M -> 20.33M at the 2009/2010 boundary and by each year's divPaid/shares matching its own filed DPS. Dividing all pre-2013 years would have been the error here.
SPLIT DATE: splitFacts give ratio 2 at 2012-12-31 (10-K), 2013-03-31 (10-Q) and 2013-12-31 (10-K) but no effective date, so splitAdjustments.date is recorded as the year 2013 only, not a precise day.

FY2009 DPS is sourced from CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared (0.90), not the CashPaid tag used for all other years; justified because declared equals cash-paid exactly in both overlapping years (FY2010 0.98 = 2 x 0.49, FY2011 1.06 = 2 x 0.53).

DPS TAG IS CASH-PAID, NOT DECLARED: CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid measures dividends actually paid in the fiscal year, so each year's figure lags the declared rate by roughly one quarter. FY2025 = 1.55 (Q1-Q3 at 0.385 plus Q4 at 0.395) while the current declared run-rate is 0.395 x 4 = 1.58. Growth rates are therefore on a paid basis, marginally understating declared-rate growth.

CROSS-CHECK: divPaid/sharesBasic runs 0.9%-4.2% BELOW filed DPS in every single year (2009 -0.9%, 2010 -1.4%, 2011 -1.7%, 2012 -1.3%, 2013 -1.9%, 2014 -2.0%, 2015 -1.8%, 2016 -2.5%, 2017 -4.2%, 2018 -2.6%, 2019 -2.7%, 2020 -2.0%, 2021 -2.0%, 2022 -2.0%, 2023 -1.8%, 2024 -1.5%, 2025 -1.2%). All inside the 5% tolerance; the persistent small gap reflects weighted-average basic shares sitting below actual shares outstanding on record dates plus the paid-vs-declared timing lag. No year failed the check. These checks used DividendsCommonStockCash for FY2009-FY2013 (common only) rather than PaymentsOfDividends.

divPaid in fin uses the primary tag PaymentsOfDividends, which for FY2009-FY2013 includes preferred dividends (FY2009 9,557k vs common-only 8,802k; FY2010 10,570k vs 9,823k; FY2011 11,513k vs 10,799k; FY2012 12,757k vs 12,178k; FY2013 14,474k vs 14,431k). Payout ratios for those years are therefore overstated by up to ~8% relative to common-only. From FY2014 on the two tags are identical - preferred stock was retired after 2013.

FY2014 and FY2015 CFO are missing from the primary tag NetCashProvidedByUsedInOperatingActivities; I substituted NetCashProvidedByUsedInOperatingActivitiesContinuingOperations (82,595,000 and 183,715,000). Safe because the two tags agree to the dollar in every overlapping year (FY2012 108,969,000; FY2013 150,314,000; FY2016 212,162,000; FY2017 198,863,000). FY2014 CFO is genuinely depressed, not a tag artifact.

FY2025 equity is null - the primary equity tag StockholdersEquityIncludingPortionAttributableToNoncontrollingInterest stops at FY2024 and no StockholdersEquity values were supplied in the file (only a candidate listing). FY2025 ROIC is therefore null, including in latest.roic.
FY2009 has no debtLT/debtCur, so netDebt, netDebtToEbitda and ROIC are all null for that year (the ROIC denominator would be materially understated with debt treated as zero).

FY2009 has no pretax figure, so the 21% fallback tax rate applied - moot since FY2009 ROIC is null anyway. Deriving pretax as netIncome + tax would have implied ~35%, in line with the FY2010 effective rate of 35.4%.

Revenue is null for FY2009-FY2015: the primary revenue tag starts at FY2016 and no values for SalesRevenueNet or Revenues were supplied in the file. FCF margin is therefore only computable from FY2016 onward.

PRIOR ESTIMATES WERE WRONG AND ARE REPLACED: prior growth5y of 3% vs actual 6.52%; prior payoutPctFcf of 70% vs actual FY2025 138% (FCF payout exceeded 100% in FY2025 and was uncoverable in FY2021, FY2022 and FY2023 where FCF was negative). The prior streak of 58 years cannot be verified from this data - XBRL only reaches FY2009, giving 16 verified consecutive increases; windowLimited is true and the true streak very likely extends earlier.
payoutFcf is null in FY2010, FY2011, FY2014, FY2021, FY2022 and FY2023 because FCF was negative (heavy capex cycle: FY2021-FY2023 capex of 194M/302M/260M against a ~120M historical run-rate).
fcfGrowth5 is -25.35%/yr (FY2020 FCF 109,424,000 -> FY2025 25,368,000); both endpoints are positive so the CAGR is computable, but it spans a capex supercycle and is not a run-rate.
growth.yearsCovered is 17 fiscal years of data (FY2009-FY2025), i.e. 16 year-over-year intervals; gMax is the 16-year CAGR from 0.45 to 1.55.
coverSharesOutstanding as of 2026-08-03 is 22,732,540, slightly below FY2025 weighted basic of 22,872,000 - consistent, no split or large issuance since.

normalised.notes: Stepan Company (SCL), Dec-31 FYE, Materials. The dividend record is clean and unambiguous: a filed annual cash-paid DPS tag covers FY2010-FY2025 uninterrupted, rising every single year (0.49 -> 1.55), with FY2009 recoverable at 0.45 after the single 2:1 split adjustment. 16 consecutive verified increases, no cut, no hold, no specials, no COVID interruption. Growth is decelerating hard: 7.82%/yr over 10 years, 6.52% over 5, 4.20% over 3, and the latest raises are ~2.6%/yr (1.47 -> 1.51 -> 1.55). Coverage is what changed. Through FY2022 payout was ~16-27% of net income and mostly comfortable against FCF. Then earnings collapsed (net income 147M in FY2022 -> 40M in FY2023 -> 50M -> 47M) while the capex cycle pushed capex to 302M/260M, producing three straight years of negative FCF (FY2021-FY2023). FY2025 leaves the dividend costing 35.0M against 25.4M of FCF - a 138% FCF payout - and 75% of net income. Net debt went from -151M (net cash) in FY2020 to 494M, i.e. 2.4x EBITDA, down from 3.2x in FY2023. ROIC fell from ~15% pre-2021 to 2.8-3.5% in FY2023-FY2024 and is not computable for FY2025 (equity tag missing). The dividend is not currently funded out of free cash flow; it is funded by the balance sheet, and the shrinking raises look like management acknowledging that. Capex has already normalised to ~122M in FY2024-FY2025, so FCF recovery depends on margin recovery rather than further capex cuts.

rules.note: FY2025 dividends 35.0M vs FCF 25.4M = 1.381x. On the forward 1.58 rate (~35.9M) it is ~1.42x. rules.name: Streak long enough to prove policy, short enough to still be fast
rules.note: XBRL only reaches FY2009, giving 16 verified consecutive increases with no cut, hold or COVID interruption - that streak runs to the edge of the window, so it is window-limited. The prior research figure of 58 years is plausible for Stepan (a long-standing Dividend King). Using 58, the streak is well past the 30-year ceiling: this is a mature, slow-compounding policy, not an early-stage one. On the data-only streak of 16 the rule would pass; I used the research figure because it is the true policy length.

rules.name: Balance sheet not competing with you
rules.note: FY2025 net debt 494.0M / EBITDA 204.6M = 2.41x, improving from 3.20x in FY2023. Passes, but only just, and the swing is stark: SCL held 151M of net cash in FY2020. The balance sheet is now what funds the dividend.

rules.name: Why competitors cannot take the business
rules.note: Stepan has real scale in surfactants, a plant network placed near customers so freight economics favour it, and formulations that are qualified into customers' consumer-product recipes - which creates switching friction at the SKU level. But the honest sentence is that surfactants are sold on price against commodity feedstock costs: 3% ROIC and an earnings base that halved on volume and margin pressure is what a business without pricing power looks like.

rules.name: Management treats the dividend as a promise
rules.note: The dividend rose through FY2020 and FY2021 and in every one of the 16 years in the data. No cut, hold, suspension or special anywhere in the window. FY2008 is outside the XBRL window and cannot be checked from this data.

analysis.sectorNote: Stepan is a plain industrial/specialty-chemicals manufacturer, so no sector carve-out applies: rules 4, 7 and 8 were read straight off FCF, ROIC and net debt/EBITDA with no REIT, insurer or utility substitution. The only accommodation made is on rule 7, where FY2025 ROIC is not computable from the extract (missing equity tag) and FY2024's 3.46% was used as the standing figure.
analysis.moat: Stepan's scale and plant network in surfactants plus formulations qualified into customers' consumer-product recipes create switching friction, but the product still clears on price against commodity feedstock costs - which is why ROIC fell from ~15% to ~3%.
analysis.assessment: SCL is a $1.4B surfactants maker yielding 2.56% on the current $1.58 run-rate, with 16 verified consecutive increases in the data and very likely 58 in reality - the policy is not in doubt, but the funding is. The dividend grew 6.52%/yr over five years while the earnings behind it collapsed: net income 126.8M (FY2020) -> 46.9M (FY2025), ROIC from ~15% to 3.5%, and FCF from 109.4M to 25.4M after a capex supercycle that ran 194M/302M/260M in FY2021-FY2023. That leaves FY2025 dividends of 35.0M against 25.4M of FCF, a 138% payout (roughly 142% on the forward rate), funded from a balance sheet that swung from 151M net cash to 494M net debt at 2.41x EBITDA. The snowball here has stalled: a 2.6% raise on a 2.6% yield compounds at roughly 5%, and the runway is negative rather than merely thin. The thing most likely to break it is one more year of depressed surfactant margins - capex has already normalised to ~122M, so there is no lever left but earnings recovery, and another flat-to-down year puts a 58-year streak in front of a board that has to choose between the promise and the leverage.
strengths: 16 consecutive increases verified in the data (FY2009-FY2025), no cut, hold or special, including straight through 2020
Yield of 2.56% sits squarely in the usable band, on a clean regular quarterly dividend of 0.395
Market cap of $1.40B is small enough that a genuine earnings recovery would move the whole company
Leverage is already improving: net debt/EBITDA 3.20x (FY2023) -> 2.88x -> 2.41x, and capex has normalised to ~122M from a 302M peak
risks: FY2025 dividends of 35.0M exceed FCF of 25.4M (138%); FCF was negative outright in FY2021, FY2022 and FY2023
ROIC has fallen from 13-15% pre-2021 to 2.8-3.5%, with FY2025 not computable from the extract
Net debt went from -151M (net cash) in FY2020 to +494M; the dividend is currently funded by the balance sheet
Raises have shrunk to ~2.6%/yr (1.47 -> 1.51 -> 1.55), which reads as management already rationing the payout
No pricing power: commodity surfactant economics mean margin recovery depends on the cycle, not on company action
A 58-year streak creates pressure to keep raising past the point the cash flow supports it

normalised.notes: H.B. Fuller, 52/53-week fiscal year ending the Saturday nearest 30 November. Regular DPS is taken straight from the filed annual CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared tag for all 17 years; no splits, no specials. Dividend growth has been steady but unspectacular: 8.02%/yr over the full span, 6.17% over 10 years, 7.45% over 5, 7.94% over 3. The dividend rose every year in the window including FY2020 and FY2021, so no COVID-era cut or hold. The real story is coverage: FCF fell from 244m in FY2020 to 121m in FY2025 (-13.1%/yr) as capex roughly doubled, pushing the FCF payout ratio from 13.7% to 41.5% while dividends paid rose from 33m to 50m. Leverage remains elevated post-Royal Adhesives (net debt 1.91bn at FY2025 vs 1.66bn at FY2020) and ROIC has sat in the 5-7% range since FY2019, below the 10-15% the pre-2017 business earned.

issues.detail: Internally honest but externally misleading if consumed bare. H.B. Fuller is an externally well-documented multi-decade dividend raiser (priorEstimates' 57 is in the right ballpark for real-world history, and FMP confirms the company has been listed since 1973-02-21), yet the record exposes 16. Any downstream screen or ranking that sorts on consecutiveIncreasesInData without reading streak.windowLimited will place FUL alongside a 16-year raiser and materially under-rank it. The record flags this correctly in dataQuality but the numeric field itself carries no guard.
issues.suggested: Keep 16 as the verified-in-window value but surface it as a floor, e.g. consecutiveIncreasesInData: 16 with a companion field streakIsFloor: true / streakDisplay: "16+ (window-limited; history predates FY2009 data window, prior estimate ~57)". Do not overwrite 16 with 57 — it is unverified here.

The null is a data gap masquerading as an absence of risk.
issues.suggested: Carry the FY2024 value forward as an explicit stale/proxy figure rather than null, or compute an approximate FY2025 ratio from the FY2024 EBITDA level: 1,909,724,000 / ~439,000,000 ≈ 4.35x (flag as estimated). At minimum add latest.netDebtToEbitdaAsOf: "2024" / leverageFlag: true so the leverage risk is not lost to a null.

rules.note: live marketCap 2,734,014,101 at $50.83 (2026-09-17). Well inside the ideal band; a mid-cap adhesives formulator with room to compound.

rules.note: FY2025 divPaid 50.3m / FCF 121.2m = 41.5%; on net income 33.1%. Inside the band but deteriorating fast - it was 13.7% of FCF in FY2020. Direction of travel is the concern, not the level.

rules.name: Streak long enough to prove policy, short enough to stay fast
rules.note: XBRL window starts FY2009 and shows 16 consecutive increases running back to the first year in the data, so the data streak is window-limited. Prior research streak of 57 years is plausible for H.B. Fuller (NYSE-listed since 1973) and is the figure used. At ~57 years this is a mature, slow-compounding policy - it fails the upper bound, which is exactly consistent with the sub-8% growth in rule 3.

rules.name: Earnings growing at least as fast as the dividend
rules.note: FCF fell 244.3m (FY2020) to 121.2m (FY2025) as capex roughly doubled (87m -> 142m). FY2014 CFO is a known outlier but is not an endpoint here, so the comparison stands. Cross-check on net income (123.7m -> 152.0m = +4.20%/yr) also falls short of 7.45%. The dividend has been growing on a shrinking cash base for five years.

rules.name: High return on invested capital
rules.note: FY2025 ROIC is null because FY2025 OperatingIncomeLoss is missing from the filings data. FY2024 6.56%, FY2023 6.25%, FY2022 6.85% - ROIC has sat in the 5-7% band every year since FY2019, versus 10-15% for the pre-Royal-Adhesives business. Roughly half the hurdle.

rules.name: Balance sheet not competing with you
rules.note: FY2025 net debt is 1.91bn but EBITDA is null for lack of FY2025 operating income; holding FY2024 EBITDA of 439.3m gives ~4.35x. FY2024 actual 4.19x, FY2023 3.81x. Leverage has been above 3.8x every year since the 2017 Royal Adhesives deal and is rising again, not falling. This trips the >4x avoid trigger.

rules.name: Why competitors cannot take the business
rules.note: Adhesives are a low single-digit share of a customer's bill of materials but sit in the middle of a qualified production line; re-qualifying a substitute means re-validating line speed, cure and shelf life, so incumbency is sticky. Consistent with 3.5bn of revenue held roughly flat through a destocking cycle rather than lost on price.

rules.name: Management treats the dividend as a promise
rules.note: FY2020 0.648 > FY2019 0.635 and FY2021 0.665 > FY2020 - raised straight through COVID. No cut, hold or suspension anywhere in the FY2009-FY2025 window. 2008 sits outside the XBRL window and cannot be checked from this data.

analysis.assessment: FUL offers a 1.83% starting yield on the FY2025 declared rate of $0.928 growing 7.45%/yr - a roughly 9.3% arithmetic snowball before multiple change, which is respectable but not the 12%+ a $2.7bn compounder should deliver. The 41.5% FCF payout still looks like runway until you see how it got there: free cash flow fell from $244m in FY2020 to $121m in FY2025 (-13.1%/yr) while dividends paid rose from $33m to $50m, so coverage thinned by shrinking the numerator, not by outgrowing it. The balance sheet is what breaks the case - net debt of $1.91bn against roughly $439m of EBITDA is about 4.3x, above 3.8x every year since the 2017 Royal Adhesives acquisition, while ROIC has been stuck at 5-7% versus the 10-15% the pre-deal business earned. Management has raised the dividend for ~57 straight years and did not flinch in FY2020, so the promise is real; the question is whether the cash to fund it is. The single thing most likely to break this is the leverage: at 4.3x with capex running $142m a year, any EBITDA slip forces a choice between deleveraging and the raise, and the raise is the smaller number.
analysis.moat: Industrial adhesives specified into customer production lines, where switching means re-qualifying line speed, cure and shelf life for a component that is a tiny share of the bill of materials.
strengths: Market cap $2.73bn - small enough that incremental wins still move the needle
16 consecutive raises verifiable in data (FY2009-FY2025), ~57 by prior research, including straight through FY2020 and FY2021
FCF payout 41.5% and NI payout 33.1% - the dividend is not the immediate binding constraint
Revenue held near $3.5bn through a destocking cycle, consistent with specification lock-in rather than price competition
risks: Net debt/EBITDA ~4.3x (FY2024 4.19x), above 3.8x in every year since the FY2017 Royal Adhesives acquisition
FCF -13.1%/yr over five years while the dividend grew 7.45%/yr - coverage is eroding from the cash side
ROIC 5-7% since FY2019, roughly half the 12% hurdle and far below the 10-15% the pre-2017 business earned
Capex has roughly doubled since FY2020 ($87m -> $142m) with no FCF payoff visible yet
5-yr DPS growth of 7.45% is below the 8% gate and has been below it on a 10-year view too
analysis.sectorNote: Specialty chemicals - all ten rules are a fair fit, no REIT/insurer/utility adjustment needed. FCF = CFO - capex is the right payout basis. One caveat: FY2025 EBITDA, net debt/EBITDA and ROIC are null in the source because FY2025 OperatingIncomeLoss is missing from the filings; rules 7 and 8 were assessed on FY2024 (ROIC 6.56%, 4.19x) plus an FY2025 leverage estimate of 1,909.7m / 439.3m = 4.35x carried on FY2024 EBITDA. The null is a data gap, not an absence of leverage, and was not allowed to pass the rule by default. FY2010-FY2014 net debt is a lower bound (current debt absent from the join) and FY2014 CFO of 29.7m is a suspect outlier - neither affects any figure used above.

normalised.dpsMethod: Filed annual DPS tags with ~1-year durations, spliced: FY2016-FY2025 from CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared (10-K FY facts, 364-365 days); FY2008-FY2015 from CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid (10-K FY facts), the only annual DPS tag before 2016, which matches the declared tag exactly in the 2016/2017 overlap (0.34 / 0.36). FY2008-FY2014 were then divided by 2 for the 2017 2-for-1 split; FY2015 onward were already filed on the post-split basis (the FY2015 annual fact of 0.32 comes from the post-split restatement window, while that year's own quarterly facts of 0.16 x4 = 0.64 are pre-split). No adjustment for the 2010 2-for-1 split: FY2008-FY2009 are already on the post-2010 basis (FY2009 divPaid 29,352k / filed basic shares 76,351k = 0.3844 = filed DPS 0.38).

splitAdjustments.note: 2-for-1 split reported across the 2017 filings (StockholdersEquityNoteStockSplitConversionRatio1 = 2 at 2017-03-31 10-Q, 2017-05-03 and 2017-06-30; exact effective date not in the data, 2017-05-03 is the earliest dated split fact). Basis boundary evidence: cover CommonStockSharesOutstanding 55,051,158 at the FY2016 10-K vs 110,385,344 at the FY2017 10-K; weighted basic shares step from 63,426k (FY2014) to 122,042k (FY2015). The FY2017 10-K restatement window (2017 plus the two prior years 2016 and 2015) is therefore already post-split, so only FY2014 and earlier were adjusted (DPS/2, shares x2) - seven years, exactly consistent with the three-year window. After adjustment, divPaid/shares vs adjusted DPS agrees within 1.5% in all seven years (FY2014 0.3045 vs 0.30; FY2013 0.2817 vs 0.28; FY2009 0.1922 vs 0.19).

Second 2-for-1 split (StockholdersEquityNoteStockSplitConversionRatio = 2, FY2010 10-K; cover shares 38,283,852 at the FY2009 10-K vs 69,875,873 at the FY2010 10-K). NO years adjusted: the window starts at FY2008 and both FY2008 and FY2009 are already restated onto the post-2010 basis (FY2009 29,352k/76,351k = 0.3844 = filed 0.38; FY2008 26,003k / 0.34 implies ~76.5m shares). Dividing them again would be a double adjustment.

analysis.assessment: SLGN is a $4.1bn packager paying a 2.07% yield on 0.80 of regular DPS with only 20.3% of FY2025 free cash flow committed to it, so the payout itself is in no danger - dividends paid were 85.8m against 422.7m of FCF. The snowball is a modest-yield, historically double-digit-growth one (10.76% 5-yr DPS CAGR), but it is visibly slowing: 7.72% over three years and just +5% in the 2026 raise, so a 2% starting yield compounding at mid-single digits is a slower engine than the headline suggests. The thing most likely to break it is the balance sheet, not the payout: net debt has climbed from $2.04bn (FY2019) to $3.27bn (FY2025) while FCF compounded only 2.25% a year over five years, and the last computable leverage and return figures were 3.61x net debt/EBITDA and 9.0% ROIC - acquisitions, not operating returns, are doing the growing. Four quality metrics (ROIC, net debt/EBITDA, revenue, earnings payout) are null in the latest year because the XBRL join drops operating income, equity, revenue and net income after FY2019/FY2020, so rules 7 and 8 are judged on the FY2016-FY2019 trend plus the derivable net-debt figure. Seven of ten rules pass: a legitimate candidate on dividend policy and coverage, held back from 'strong' by the gap between 10.8% dividend growth and 2.3% cash-flow growth on rising leverage.

normalised.notes: Landstar (FYE = last Saturday of December, tagged --12-31) is an asset-light freight broker with a small, fast-growing regular dividend plus a near-annual December special. Regular DPS compounds at 12.4% (3yr), 14.6% (5yr), 17.9% (10yr) and 14.5% over the full 17-year window, with 11 consecutive annual increases from FY2015 to FY2025 and no COVID-era cut. The headline filed DPS (3.56 in FY2025) is roughly 2.3x the regular (1.56) because of the recurring 2.00 special paid every year since FY2019; the FY2012/2014/2017 specials were 0.50/1.00/1.50. FY2013-FY2014 is a distorted pair: the filed FY2013 declaration of 0.35 is carried at face value and produces an apparent 26% step down to 0.26 in FY2014, but the underlying quarterly rate never fell (0.06 in Q3-2012, still 0.06 in Q1/Q2-2014, 0.07 from Q3-2014), so this is almost certainly a declaration-timing artifact of the December-2012 tax acceleration rather than a real cut - it is flagged, not smoothed. Balance sheet is net cash in every year since FY2013 on tagged debt only (-396.7M, -2.0x EBITDA in FY2025); finance-lease obligations are outside the tagged debt family, so those readings are an upper bound on net cash. FY2025 is a cyclical trough: revenue -1.6%, net income -41%, EBITDA 198.0M vs 628.5M at the FY2022 peak, FCF 215.0M (4.5% of revenue), ROIC 29% vs 79% in FY2022. Total declared dividends exceeded net income in FY2025 (106%), but the regular dividend alone is 47% of trough earnings and 25% of FCF, so the regular is well covered and the special is the discretionary, cycle-sensitive piece. REPAIR: FY2013 regular DPS changed from the inferred 0.24 to the filed 0.35 and its 0.11 'special' removed (reviewer block sustained - 0.24 was unfiled and contradicted by divPaid/shares of 0.3458); streak cut from 17 to 11 (FY2015-FY2025), windowLimited flipped to false, and an FY2014 cut 0.35 -> 0.26 recorded (reviewer block sustained); FY2009-FY2012 ROIC restated off the 21% fallback onto implied effective rates of 36.1/36.3/36.9/35.4% (0.4341/0.3159/0.3869/0.3618 -> 0.3511/0.2549/0.3089/0.2959); growth.yearsCovered corrected 18 -> 17 to match the CAGR horizon; FY2013 netIncome repaired from an internally impossible 146,009k to 108,922k (= filed pretax less filed tax, confirmed by $2.36 diluted EPS), moving FY2013 payoutNi to 0.1462 - an error neither reviewer caught; FY2013/2014/2015 payoutFcf flagged low-confidence on the substituted CFO tag; netDebt from FY2014 on and FY2009 flagged as a lower bound on leverage; regular-basis FY2025 payout (47% of NI, 25% of FCF) and the 1.60 forward run-rate added to issues. Values NOT changed: all FY2014-FY2025 regular DPS (each re-derived independently from the filed quarterly facts and unchanged), splitAdjustments (still empty - confirmed no split), latest.dps 1.56 (FY2025 realised; 1.60 is the forward run rate, documented separately), and every g3/g5/g10/gMax figure (none of their windows touches FY2013-FY2014).

The field is ambiguous and invites a wrong restatement of the headline growth rate.

Net-cash readings from FY2014 on are an upper bound, as the record states, but the values are still published as point estimates and feed the 'net cash in every year since FY2013' claim in notes.

The record explains this in issues but the 'latest' block - the part most likely to be consumed downstream - carries no regular-basis equivalent.
